BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics

Michael Gastegger†, Adam E. Foster†, José Jiménez-Luna†, Tim Hempel†, Sarah Lewis†, Yu Xie†, Lixin Sun†, Iryna Zaporozhets†, J. Thorben Frank†, Yaoyi Chen†, Michael Plainer†, Ludwig Winkler†, Pedro B. P. S. Reis†, Sven H. Giese†, Roberto Sordillo, Victor García Satorras, Eray Inanc, Kacper Kapuśniak, Soojung Yang, Rishwanth Raghu, Rachel Kim, Gabriel Dernbach, Deniz Gunceler, Hannes Schulz, Bonnie Kruft, Marwin Segler, Christopher M. Bishop, Cecilia Clementi, Ryota Tomioka, Frank Noé* † Equal contribution *Correspondence to franknoe@microsoft.com
Abstract

Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

1 Introduction

Proteins, DNA and RNA form the basic building blocks of life, performing functions from oxygen transport and muscle contraction to storing and processing genetic information. Their activities combine three recurring processes: (i) conformational changes, which alter a molecule’s three-dimensional arrangement; (ii) binding and dissociation, which assemble complexes and capture or release ligands; and (iii) chemical reactions, which transform substrates or act as molecular switches. These processes are often coupled. In haemoglobin for example, oxygen binding shifts the conformational equilibrium from the low-affinity tense (T) state toward the high-affinity relaxed (R) state. This coupling supports cooperative oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading at the lower oxygen partial pressures in tissues [1]. In adenylate kinase, the catalytic cycle connects nucleotide binding, domain closure, phosphoryl transfer and reopening for product release [2]. These molecular activities form interconnected pathways that underpin cellular function. A scalable means of understanding molecular function and its disruption in disease could transform drug-target selection, clarify mechanisms of action, and improve predictions of drug efficacy and safety.

Next-generation sequencing has made molecular sequences broadly accessible [3], while AlphaFold, RoseTTAFold and their all-atom extensions have transformed the prediction of molecular structures and complexes [4, 5, 6, 7]. A predicted structure alone, however, does not specify which conformations are populated, how rapidly they interconvert, or how ligand binding changes these properties. Understanding function therefore requires information about structural ensembles and their dynamics.

Biophysical experiments can reveal many aspects of biomolecular function, but usually suffer from either low throughput or low resolution. E.g., cryo-electron microscopy can resolve different conformational states, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy measures structural fluctuations and exchange processes [8, 9], but both are expensive and require lengthy sample preparation, data collection and data analysis. A broad range of biophysical techniques probe biomolecular shape, dynamics and interactions, including fluorescence and infrared spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry [10, 11, 12, 13]. Cell-free expression, miniaturization and cDNA display expand the scale of functional characterization, enabling high-throughput measurements of biochemical activity and protein stability [14, 15]. Even when scaled up, these approaches measure low-dimensional observables rather than directly resolving the full atomistic conformational ensemble.

Atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) describes the detailed time-resolved evolution of biomolecular structure subject to a chosen force field. Its predictive power is limited by the accuracy of the interaction potential, but especially by the computational cost of adequate sampling. Folding, conformational rearrangements and association can involve rare barrier crossings, requiring extensive simulation timescales, as illustrated by simulations of protein folding and protein–protein association [16, 17]. Specialized hardware and enhanced sampling algorithms extend the accessible timescales, but the computational burden of exploring complex conformational landscapes still remains high [16, 17, 18]. Machine-learned coarse-grained models reduce this burden by learning effective interactions for fewer degrees of freedom [19, 20]. Recent transferable models reproduce structural and thermodynamic properties of atomistic simulations while achieving orders-of-magnitude computational savings on benchmark proteins [20]. Yet extending this accuracy across small molecules, recovering atomistic detail and calibrating kinetics remain challenging.

Generative models learn to directly sample a target distribution rather than resolving every intervening simulation step. Boltzmann generators sample distributions defined by known energy functions [21] but have limited capability to scale to large systems. DiG, AlphaFlow and BioEmu learn molecular ensembles from data [22, 23, 24], but are coarse-grained single-protein models. Timewarp, MDGen and implicit transfer operators extend this approach to time-separated configurations or trajectory segments [25, 26, 27], but neither of these are biomolecular foundation models that can generalize over a wide range of complex structures.

Here we introduce BioEmu2, which unifies three modes in one atomistic framework: (1) structure prediction, with accuracy comparable to current open-weight biomolecular folding models [28, 29, 30, 31] on FoldBench and Runs N’ Poses [32, 33]. (2) approximate room-temperature equilibrium sampling reproducing free energy surfaces of extensive MD simulations within 1 kcal/mol free energy error and covering the major minima; (3) time propagation, which allows structures to be propagated an arbitrary time lag τ\tau in the future, to emulate long-timescale MD trajectories and predict kinetics of conformational changes and binding. BioEmu2 supports multicomponent systems containing proteins, DNA, RNA, modified residues, ligands and ions at heavy-atom resolution. Context parallelism enables inference on systems with over 5000 residues. Contact conditioning and inference-time steering provide control over structure generation. Enhanced sampling improves coverage of rare states, and valid reweighting can recover statistics of the learned base ensemble. Several capabilities remain experimental, particularly slow kinetics, and require larger high-quality experimental datasets and further validation. By accelerating many MD-style sampling tasks by orders of magnitude, BioEmu2 enables rapid iteration toward scalable emulation of biomolecular dynamics and function.

2 BioEmu2 Model

BioEmu2 is a generative model that can predict biomolecular structures, ensembles and dynamics with atomistic resolution. In contrast to the first version of BioEmu [24], BioEmu2 can model molecular systems consisting of any number of proteins, RNA/DNA, post-translational modifications, lipids, small molecules and ions (Fig. 1).

At a high level, the BioEmu2 model separates the learning problem into two complementary parts: biological reasoning in the sequence trunk and coordinate generation in the structure module [4, 5]. In the trunk, a tokenized description of the biomolecular system, 𝒮\mathcal{S}, is obtained by representing protein chains by their amino acid composition, nucleic acids via their nucleotides and other species directly by their individual constituent atoms. Protein chains are further augmented with evolutionary information in the form of multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) [34, 35]. Optional trunk conditioning inputs, 𝒞trunk\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{trunk}}, can be provided to enable inference-time control of the structure generation. These three inputs are then processed by the sequence trunk

(𝒮,MSA,𝒞trunk)\displaystyle(\mathcal{S},\mathrm{MSA},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{trunk}}) →sequence trunk ℰtrunk.\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\text{ sequence trunk }}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{trunk}}. (2.1)

BioEmu2 supports two trunk conditioning inputs: a method flag that defines the sample distribution to either aim for precise structure prediction or approximate equilibrium sampling; and a set (possibly empty) of token-to-token physical contacts that serve as a soft constraint to the model when generating structures. As a diffusion generative model [36, 37, 38], BioEmu2’s structure module does not produce structures in a single forward pass, instead it progressively denoises the structure at different noise levels σ\sigma. Thus a single pass of the structure module takes as input the cached trunk embeddings, along with the coordinates describing a partially noised structure xnoisyx_{\text{noisy}} and a noise level σ\sigma

(𝒮,ℰtrunk,𝒞dyn,xnoisy,σ)\displaystyle(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{trunk}},\mathcal{C}_{\textrm{dyn}};x_{\text{noisy}},\sigma) →structure module x^,\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\text{ structure module }}\widehat{x}, (2.2)

yielding the denoised prediction x^\widehat{x}.

Departing from earlier models in the field [5, 39], BioEmu2 also emulates dynamics. In practice, this is achieved through an optional conditioning input to the structure module 𝒞dyn=(xt,τ)\mathcal{C}_{\textrm{dyn}}=(x_{t},\tau). This carries the starting structure xtx_{t} and a time lag τ>0\tau>0. The model is then trained to sample the distribution pτ​(xt+τ|xt)p_{\tau}(x_{t+\tau}|x_{t}), i.e. the structural distribution starting in xtx_{t} and propagating MD simulation forwards in time over an interval τ\tau.

Inference modes.

The possibility of different conditioning inputs for the sequence trunk and the structure module give raise to three primary combinations of inference modes which are summarized below:

  • •

    Structure prediction (method = structure prediction, 𝒞dyn=∅\mathcal{C}_{\textrm{dyn}}=\varnothing): The structure module generates predicted structures x^\widehat{x} that mimics static structures obtained by X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM experiments.

  • •

    Equilibrium sampling (method = equilibrium, 𝒞dyn=∅\mathcal{C}_{\textrm{dyn}}=\varnothing): generates conformational samples from a learned approximation to the equilibrium distribution.

  • •

    Time propagation / dynamics (method = equilibrium, 𝒞dyn=(xt,τ)\mathcal{C}_{\textrm{dyn}}=(x_{t},\tau)): Simulates temporal evolution of initial structures xtx_{t} for a time lag τ\tau, to time-propagated structures x∼pτ​(xt+τ|xt)x\sim p_{\tau}(x_{t+\tau}|x_{t}).

We note that it is possible to set inputs to the model that combine dynamics conditioning with structure prediction inference mode, but this is not recommended as no training data example uses this. MSA computation and trunk embedding are typically more expensive than an individual structure module evaluation. BioEmu2 therefore computes trunk embeddings ℰtrunk\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{trunk}} once and reuses them across many samples or propagation steps.

3 Results

We start this section by verifying the competitive performance of BioEmu2 for static structure prediction on established co-folding benchmarks and probe the scalability of our inference to large structures. We then analyse the performance of BioEmu2 for equilibrium sampling before turning to its modelling of biomolecular kinetics. Finally, we highlight how steering and enhanced sampling techniques offer inference-time control over the obtained ensembles and the quality of generated structures.

3.1 Structure Prediction

FoldBench and Runs N’ Poses.

We first assess BioEmu2’s ability to predict accurate individual biomolecular structures. In structure prediction mode, the model targets structures characteristic of experimental structure data, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, rather than an equilibrium ensemble. Using this setting, we compare BioEmu2 to a range of co-folding baseline models on the popular FoldBench benchmark suite [32] and the Runs N’ Poses benchmark [33] for protein–ligand bound structure prediction. We selected models for comparison that have a suitable commercial license (excludes AlphaFold3 [5]) and a comparable training data cut-off (excludes Boltz-2 [39]), resulting in the following baseline methods: Boltz-1 [28], ESMFold2 [31], OpenFold3 [40], Protenix v1 and v2 [29] and OpenDDE [30]. We do not use confidence heads when aggregating over multiple samples. The full details of our versions of the two benchmarks are described in Sec. 4.8.

Across both benchmarks, BioEmu2 achieves accuracy competitive with the evaluated co-folding baselines, establishing structure prediction as a core capability of our model (Fig. 2a,b). Specifically, in the FoldBench results we see that BioEmu2 achieves competitive lDDT [41] scores for protein and nucleic acid monomers, and attains strong DockQ-based [42] success rates for chain-to-chain binding. The higher score for protein–protein binding is likely driven by the training data composition, which emphasized protein–protein interaction. The protein–ligand evaluation from Runs N’ Poses also highlights the ability of BioEmu2 to model ligand placement alongside the surrounding protein structure [33] at a performance level comparable to other strong models. In the comparison presented in Section 3.4, physicality-steered sampling largely preserves structural prediction accuracy, with modest gains in some categories (Fig. 6b).

Scaling inference to large complexes.

BioEmu2’s structural prediction capability extends to larger molecular assemblies. To make larger biomolecular systems accessible at inference time, BioEmu2 implements context parallelism (CP) to distribute pair representations across multiple GPUs [43]. Benchmarks on NVIDIA B200 GPUs demonstrate scaling from a single GPU to 4 GPUs (2×22\times 2) and 16 GPUs (4×44\times 4) configurations, supporting systems of up to approximately 16,000 residues. Figure 2c shows that our CP code substantially extends the maximum accessible system size with manageable communication overhead. At this size, the physicality of the prediction becomes more of a bottleneck than computational feasibility.

BioEmu2 preserves both local structural accuracy and overall assembly organization for a wide range of large protein complexes containing thousands of residues. Examples include four multimeric complexes in the test set: 9ISQ (3,508 residues), 8DOL (3,558 residues), 9Q3J (4,040 residues) and 8WW8 (5,832 residues), achieving backbone lDDT scores of 0.81, 0.87, 0.94, and 0.80, global RMSDs of 5.5Å, 5.7 Å, 2.0Å and 6.6 Å respectively (Fig. 2d).

The probability to get successful structure prediction out of the box tends to decrease for increasingly large complexes—both because the structure prediction problem is harder, and because it is often not well-defined as large complexes tend to be assembled in the cell rather than forming in solution. In this case, providing a few additional hints such as residue–residue contacts obtained from experimental knowledge can be sufficient to substantially improve BioEmu2’s predictions. As an example, for the 4,020-residue complex 8WY8, specifying just a single inter-chain contact dramatically improves prediction accuracy, reducing RMSD from 71.2 Å to 5.0 Å and increasing DockQ from 0.10 to 0.46 (Fig. 2e).

3.2 Equilibrium Sampling

In equilibrium mode, BioEmu2 generates independent draws from a learned structural distribution for the specified system. Instead of targeting sharp single-state predictions, this mode aims at reproducing the distribution of structures in acqueous solvent at ambient conditions (room temperature and atmospheric pressure). This typically leads to higher flexibility and more shallow energy minima than in structure prediction mode (Fig 3a).

BioEmu2 is a Boltzmann emulator: unlike Boltzmann Generators [21], which sample from a distribution pe​q​(x)p_{eq}(x) specified by a known force field, it learns to sample an approximation to pθ​(x)p_{\theta}(x) from data, generalizing across proteins and biomolecular systems. This follows earlier data-driven ensemble models, including AlphaFlow [23] and BioEmu [24]. Formally,

x∼pθ​(x|𝒮)pθ​(x|𝒮)≈pe​q​(x|𝒮)x\sim p_{\theta}(x|\mathcal{S})\qquad p_{\theta}(x|\mathcal{S})\approx p_{eq}(x|\mathcal{S}) (3.1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the molecular system, xx are the 3D coordinates of all heavy atoms, and pθp_{\theta} is BioEmu2’s equilibrium distribution aiming to approximate the ground truth equilibrium distribution pe​qp_{eq}. pθp_{\theta} is learned from the structure distribution generated by explicit-solvent all-atom MD simulations at 300K temperature and 11 atm pressure in the isothermal-isobaric (N​p​TNpT) ensemble using Amber force fields [44]. Solvent and simulation volume are marginalized out, so solvent effects are implicitly learned by the model.

Free energy surfaces.

To compare BioEmu2’s pθp_{\theta} distribution with the MD data ground truth distribution pe​qp_{eq}, we first project samples from both distributions onto the two collective variables that govern the slowest transition processes of each test system, computed by time-lagged independent component analysis (TICA) [45, 46]. This projection resolves the metastable (long-lived) states which (i) have potentially biological relevance, e.g. as conformations selected by binding partners, and (ii) represent a more challenging and informative test when comparing pθp_{\theta} and pe​qp_{eq} rather than fast or local fluctuation metrics [47]. We compute and compare free energy surfaces U⁡(x)=−kB​T​ln⁡pY​(x)U(x)=-k_{B}T\ln p_{Y}(x) where pY​(x)p_{Y}(x) is the 2D-TICA density from either MD or BioEmu2 (Fig. 3)

Free energy error

measures how accurately the model reproduces the relative populations of metastable states. Let qne​qq^{eq}_{n} and qnθq_{n}^{\theta} denote the relative populations of metastable state nn in the reference and model distributions, respectively, obtained by integrating pe​qp_{eq} and pθp_{\theta} over the corresponding region of configuration space and normalizing. We subsequently report the mean absolute error over the MM metastable states found in the TICA projection:

MAEF=kB​TM​∑n|ln⁡qnθ−ln⁡qne​q|.\mathrm{MAE}_{F}=\frac{k_{B}T}{M}\sum_{n}\left|\ln q_{n}^{\theta}-\ln q^{eq}_{n}\right|. (3.2)

State coverage

instead measures how much of the reference conformational space is sampled by the model, normalized for sample count. We finely discretize the two-dimensional TICA space into states and report

coverage=|Cθ∩Cref|c~ref​(N),\mathrm{coverage}=\frac{|C_{\theta}\cap C_{\mathrm{ref}}|}{\widetilde{c}_{\mathrm{ref}}(N)}, (3.3)

where CθC_{\theta} and CrefC_{\mathrm{ref}} are the model-visited and reference-visited state sets, and c~ref​(N)\widetilde{c}_{\mathrm{ref}}(N) is the expected number of distinct states visited by an equally sized sample drawn independently from the reference distribution. Coverage equals one when the model matches the expected reference coverage.

Together, these metrics capture whether BioEmu2 both finds the relevant conformational states and reproduces their relative populations.

Sampling modes and functional dynamics.

BioEmu2 allows to choose between standard structure prediction and equilibrium sampling. We probe the effect of the two modes on the example of adenylate kinase, which exhibits a large conformational change upon substrate binding. Using BioEmu2 in structure prediction and equilibrium sampling mode, we generate conformations for the Apo (PDB structure 4AKE), the ATP-bound and the AMP+ATP-bound (PDB structure 1AKE) state (Fig. 3a). In both modes, BioEmu2 samples structures close to the apo and the holo state, where the relative weight between sampled conformations shifts notably when adding ATP and AMP+ATP to the system, which is in line with experimentally measured PDB structures (stars). By switching between the modes, BioEmu2 transitions from narrowly distributed structure prediction to a continuously distributed ensemble of states, which captures the nature of thermal fluctuations in a biomolecular system. We run the subsequent experiments in equilibrium sampling mode and quantitatively assess the quality of the ensembles generated by BioEmu2.

Emulation of molecular dynamics.

We now evaluate how BioEmu2 performs on a set of test systems representing different important biomolecular modalities: single proteins, protein dimers, and protein–small molecule systems. BioEmu2 samples around 50% of states found by MD for proteins and protein complexes, and on average over 100%, i.e. more states than sampled by and equally sized sample of MD frames for protein–ligand systems (Fig. 3b). Amongst sampled states, the free energy error is in the range of 0.7 to 1.2 kcal/mol (Fig. 3b). BioEmu2 strongly outperforms models that have not been trained on MD data in terms of both coverage and free energy error (Proteinx v2 and Boltz-2 default mode shown as examples). BioEmu1 is still best on single protein dynamics, likely because it has been fine-tuned on experimental protein stabilities which is not yet the case for the current BioEmu2 release. However, BioEmu1 is a single protein model and therefore unable to compete in the protein–protein and protein–ligand categories. Boltz-2 has a MD mode and in that mode achieves close to BioEmu2 performance on state coverage, but BioEmu2 as significantly lower free energy error.

Fig 3c shows TICA landscapes and structures for three concrete example systems and compares them to the MD reference. BioEmu2 consistently matches the TICA landscapes, finding all modes and reasonably approximating their relative proportions, though often with slightly lower energy barriers between metastable states. In the example of a protein–peptide system, we find both the two peptide binding modes as well as an unbound mode, all three of which are also found in the MD reference. Furthermore, for randomly selected examples of a strong and a weak small-molecule binder, BioEmu2 qualitatively matches expectations with regard to the structural ensemble: for the strong binder, all samples are in the bound state and match the crystal structure (2AM9). For the weak binder, both bound and unbound structures are sampled, with the ligand diffusing over the protein surface in the unbound state.

3.3 Dynamics and Kinetics

Molecular kinetics can be described by the transition density pτ​(y∣x)p_{\tau}(y\mid x), the probability density of observing configuration yy a physical time τ\tau after configuration xx. It defines a transfer operator that propagates ensembles of configurations forward in time. Recent transferable generative models such as Timewarp [25], MDGen [26] and implicit transfer operators (ITO) [27, 48] implicitly learn this density and can sample future configurations directly. BioEmu2 follows this approach and samples

xt+τ∼pθ,τ(⋅∣xt),x_{t+\tau}\sim p_{\theta,\tau}(\,\cdot\mid x_{t}), (3.4)

where pθ,τp_{\theta,\tau} is learned from pairs of configurations (xt,xt+τ)(x_{t},x_{t+\tau}) that are a time lag τ\tau apart in MD trajectories. The model generates the endpoint xt+τx_{t+\tau} without resolving the motion in between, and iterating this step yields trajectories with time steps many orders of magnitude longer than the femtosecond integration step of MD.

For ergodic physical dynamics, the transition density pτ​(y∣x)p_{\tau}(y\mid x) loses memory of the starting configuration xx at sufficiently long lags τ\tau and approaches the equilibrium distribution pe​q​(y)p_{eq}(y). With a suitable parametrization (Sec. 4.6), BioEmu2 reproduces this limit and thereby unifies its transfer operator and its equilibrium distribution in one model. As the timescales of τ\tau increase, time propagation thus turns continuously into equilibrium sampling within the same network, and loses all memory of the starting configuration for τ≫1​ms\tau\gg 1\,\mathrm{ms}. Despite this asymptotic limit, predictions of slower binding, dissociation, folding, unfolding and other rearrangements are not established as quantitatively accurate kinetics in the current BioEmu2 release.

Autocorrelations on MD timescales.

Matching equilibrium distributions does not necessarily imply realistic dynamics, because different dynamics can yield the same equilibrium. A direct test for dynamics is whether BioEmu2 trajectories decorrelate as quickly as MD along the slowest motions that MD reveals. To test this, we compare BioEmu2 ITO trajectories with MD for 78 systems: CATH domains, PDBbind protein–ligand complexes and protein heterodimers (Fig. 4). For each system, we project the MD trajectories and 100 BioEmu2 trajectories onto the two slowest TICA coordinates of MD, IC1 and IC2. The autocorrelation C⁡(τ)C(\tau) decays to zero as the trajectories lose memory of earlier configurations, and a faster decay means faster dynamics along that coordinate. For most systems, the difference from MD at τ=100​ns\tau=100\,\mathrm{ns} lies within the range of differences between random halves of the MD data; where it is larger, BioEmu2 mostly decays faster (Fig. 4). The differences are similar whether 100​ns100\,\mathrm{ns} is covered by one step of τ=100​ns\tau=100\,\mathrm{ns} or by 100 steps of τ=1​ns\tau=1\,\mathrm{ns}, with no clear sign that errors accumulate over many steps. Generally, we observe that BioEmu2 comes close to MD for many systems, but sometimes relaxes too quickly.

Ligand-coupled domain closure of adenylate kinase.

We emulate MD simulations with BioEmu2 by generating sequential rollouts (x0x_{0}, xτ1x_{\tau_{1}}, xτ1+τ2x_{\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}}, …\dots, xTx_{T}). Here one can choose the lag times equally, τ1=τ2=⋯\tau_{1}=\tau_{2}=\cdots, or differently, e.g. to finely resolve initial relaxation processes and make long time steps later to cover a large timescale TT. We first illustrate Adenylate kinase (ADK), a classic example of ligand binding coupled to large domain motions: its LID and NMP domains close over ATP and AMP to form the catalytically active state [49, 2]. Equilibrium sampling with BioEmu2 captures the ligand-dependent states of ADK (Fig. 3a) but not the order in which the ligands bind and the domains close. In the trajectory shown, at a lag of 50​ns50\,\mathrm{ns} (Fig. 5a–c), we place ATP⋅\cdotMg2+ and AMP beside the open apo enzyme, each closer to the binding site of the other. Within 3​μ​s3\,\mu\mathrm{s}, both ligands find their own sites and then ATP stays mostly bound, whereas the NMP domain takes almost 30​μ​s30\,\mu\mathrm{s} until it closes over AMP, followed by the LID less than 1​μ​s1\,\mu\mathrm{s} later. At 43​μ​s43\,\mu\mathrm{s}, the enzyme is within 0.1​nm0.1\,\mathrm{nm} Cα\alpha RMSD of the closed crystal structure 1ANK [49], with both ligands in their crystallographic poses (Fig. 5c). Across 50 trajectories, about 40% close within 50​μ​s50\,\mu\mathrm{s} when the ligands are present, but none when ligands are not present (Fig. 5d). BioEmu2 thus propagates the enzyme together with its ligands and Mg2+ through coupled binding and domain closure, and it provides testable predictions about the mechanism of ligand-induced conformational transitions.

Coupled folding and binding of PUMA to MCL-1.

Many intrinsically disordered proteins fold only when they bind with a partner, and the routes by which they reach their bound structure are difficult to observe directly. The BH3 domain of PUMA is disordered on its own and folds into a helix as it binds the groove of the protein MCL-1, which makes it a model system for coupled folding and binding [50, 51, 20]. We investigate if BioEmu2 finds the native complex when PUMA starts outside the groove, and by which route. We run 500 trajectories of a total of T=6.5​msT=6.5\,\mathrm{ms} each from one starting structure, with a lag that grows from 1​ns1\,\mathrm{ns} to 5​μ​s5\,\mu\mathrm{s}, adding up to more than 3​s3\,\mathrm{s} of simulated time. In the trajectory shown (Fig. 5e–g), PUMA explores the surface of MCL-1 for about 100​μ​s100\,\mu\mathrm{s} and then folds into a helix in the groove, which settles seven residues (about two helical turns) out of register. This misregistered helix persists for more than half a millisecond until, within a single 1​μ​s1\,\mu\mathrm{s} step, it snaps into the native register, and D146 of PUMA forms a salt bridge. PUMA then stays in the native register, ending close to the NMR structure 2ROC [50]. Of 500 trajectories, 78% bind (Fig. 5h), and about three quarters of these first pass through a non-native helical intermediate state.

3.4 Steering and Enhanced Sampling

BioEmu2 sample generation can be manipulated at inference time using steering. This can be used both to enhance physical quality of generated samples and to improve rare state coverage using enhanced sampling techniques [52]. Let pθ​(x)p_{\theta}(x) denote the unsteered model distribution, a potential funtion v⁡(x)v(x) defines a desired tilted distribution,

pv​(x)∝pθ​(x)​exp⁡[−v⁡(x)].p_{v}(x)\propto p_{\theta}(x)\exp[-v(x)]. (3.5)

Potentials can penalize geometric defects, favour contacts or reference conformations, or target a range of a collective variable. For physicality steering, we use guidance on detached denoised coordinates with optional Feynman-Kac resampling [28, 53]. For the enhanced sampling, we differentiate the potential through the denoiser and use a discrete transition-ratio weighting scheme adapted from the Twisted Diffusion Sampler (TDS) [54].

Physicality steering.

For structure prediction, we use geometric restraints to discourage bond distortions, steric overlaps, and stereochemical defects without imposing a particular target fold. Our implementation combines potentials derived from Boltz [28, 39] with the addition of explicit polymer geometry and clash terms, including restraints for nucleic acids (see Sec. 4.7 for details). The results in Fig. 6b compare unsteered sampling with physicality steering applied during approximately the final 20% of denoising across the FoldBench benchmark. For most categories structural accuracy benchmarks are unaffected by steering, however notable improvement of mean best-of-five lDDT is seen for DNA monomers (0.571 to 0.604) and RNA monomers (0.660 to 0.679). For individual DNA/RNA systems the improvement can be substantial (Fig. 6b, right). Across categories, significantly fewer steered samples had a polymer clash, bond-length outlier, or bond-angle outlier (Fig. 6b, bottom). For DNA and RNA monomers, the unphysical fraction decreases from 70.0% to 1.4% and from 61.3% to 4.0%, respectively.

Enhanced diffusion sampling for rare states.

Enhanced sampling is a family of methods used in MD simulation to enable free energy calculations with large free energy differences [55, 56]. The principle is to artificially increase the frequency of states that are rare in equilibrium using a bias potential, and to then reweight the biased samples so as to recover unbiased free energy differences. We apply the same principle to diffusion model sampling [52]: inference-time steering methods sush as TDS [54] or Feynman-Kac Corrector (FKC) [57] generate biased ensembles, and the multistate Bennett acceptance ratio (MBAR) [58, 59, 60] combines them to estimate the zero-bias model distribution.

We use phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) to illustrate enhanced sampling in BioEmu2 when an alternative reference conformation is known, but it is rarely covered by unsteered samples and its relative population under the model is not specified. For PGK, we define the bias potential using the relative pose of the two domains against the known closed conformation 2X13. More details are described in Section 4.7. In Fig. 6c, we compare unsteered sampling with enhanced sampling of the same total sample size. The enhanced sampling preserves a quantitatively similar free-energy landscape in the region well sampled without steering and extends farther along the closed-reference-like arm. Representative conformations illustrate the dominant upper-arm region (A), an open-reference-like conformation (B), and a closed-reference-like conformation (C).

4 Methods

4.1 Molecular System Definition

We describe a molecular system by

𝒮=(ℰ,ℐ,ℬ),\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{I},\mathcal{B}), (4.1)

where ℰ\mathcal{E} specifies the molecular entities, ℐ\mathcal{I} their chain copies, and ℬ\mathcal{B} their covalent connectivity. This separation distinguishes molecular identity from stoichiometry: two identical protein chains share an entity definition but remain distinct chains in the generated complex. The representation follows the entity-and-chain organization of PDBx/mmCIF and the all-atom modeling approach of AlphaFold 3 [5].

Chemical composition and connectivity.

The system definition supports monomers, multichain assemblies, and complexes containing proteins, RNA, DNA, modified residues, small molecules and branched components. Proteins are specified by their amino acid sequences, and RNA and DNA by their base sequences. Chemical components can be identified by a Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) code [61], which specifies atom identities, bonds and stereochemistry, or by supported text-based chemical encodings. Ligands, including lipids and ions, accept a CCD code, SMILES or InChI; SMILES and InChI describe the chemical structure directly.

Modified and noncanonical polymer residues are specified by their sequence positions and a CCD code or InChI. This replaces the chemical identity at the specified position. For example, phosphothreonine can be specified by the CCD code TPO at a threonine position.

Standard polymer links are constructed from sequence order. Additional covalent bonds can be added to specify connectivity not determined by chain order, such as disulfides or covalent links between chains. Together, the chain definitions, chain copies and covalent bonds determine the molecular topology. Branched components are representable but absent from the current training data.

Atom- and token-level representations.

The system is expanded into an atom-level graph and a token sequence, following the mixed-resolution representation used in all-atom structure prediction [5]. Conventional polymer residues each occupy one token; ligands, modified residues, and branched monomers use one token per heavy atom. Thus, tokens are computational units rather than a uniform coarse-grained description of the generated structure.

4.2 Multiple Sequence Alignments

Protein multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) provide evolutionary information complementary to molecular composition. Sequence conservation and correlated substitutions help the model identify structural constraints within proteins and across interacting chains, as in MSA-based structure-prediction methods [35, 4]. BioEmu2 uses these inputs for both structure prediction and equilibrium emulation.

Chain alignments and pairing.

An independent alignment is obtained for each distinct protein sequence. The default acquisition uses ColabFold [35] to search for MSAs. Each alignment includes the query sequence and homologous sequences aligned to its residue positions. Non-protein components do not require evolutionary alignments.

For heteromeric systems, paired alignments additionally associate homologues across protein chains, for example by matching occurrences of the two sequences within the genome of a single organism. Paired rows supply a correspondence that can inform intermolecular interactions, whilst unpaired alignments provide intrachain evolutionary context without indicating a special relationship between the separate alignments of the two chains. BioEmu2 combines both kinds of rows and records which positions originate from paired alignments.

Schematically, alignment preparation yields

{chain alignments}⟶(A,d,q)⟶MSA features,\{\text{chain alignments}\}\longrightarrow(A,d,q)\longrightarrow\text{MSA features}, (4.2)

where Ar​iA_{ri} is the aligned symbol in row rr at token position ii, dr​id_{ri} records insertion information relative to the query, and qr​iq_{ri} is a binary flag that indicates pairing. Gaps represent absent aligned positions and chains with no sequence in a given row. The concatenation of these features gives MSA feature vectors ur​iu_{ri}. A coarse summary of the MSA information is also included in the trunk via a simple mean-pooling over the MSA rows.

4.3 Sequence Trunk and Conditioning

The sequence trunk converts chemical and evolutionary inputs into trunk embeddings Etrunk=(Esingle,Epair)E_{\mathrm{trunk}}=(E_{\mathrm{single}},E_{\mathrm{pair}}). For LL tokens, the single-token and token-pair embeddings have shapes

Esingle∈ℝL×ds,Epair∈ℝL×L×dz,E_{\mathrm{single}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{s}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{pair}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L\times d_{z}}, (4.3)

where dsd_{s} and dzd_{z} are the single-token and token-pair feature dimensions, respectively. We set ds=384,dz=256d_{s}=384,d_{z}=256 in the BioEmu2 model. The trunk’s outputs depend on the molecular system, alignment, and conditioning. The conditioning inputs 𝒞trunk\mathcal{C}_{\text{trunk}} consist of a mode label m∈{equilibrium, structure prediction}m\in\{\text{equilibrium, structure prediction}\} and an optional set, ℋ\mathcal{H}, of contacts. The trunk is then evaluated as:

(Esingle,Epair)=Fθ​(𝒮,MSA,m,ℋ).(E_{\mathrm{single}},E_{\mathrm{pair}})=F_{\theta}(\mathcal{S},\mathrm{MSA},m,\mathcal{H}). (4.4)

This separation follows the representation-and-diffusion architecture of AlphaFold 3 and Boltz [5, 28]. It permits one representation calculation to support many coordinate samples with unchanged conditioning.

We use a PairMixer sequence trunk [62] that forgoes the triangular attention and single-representation updates of the PairFormer [5]. Earlier work, including Minifold [63], also showed that a simpler trunk architecture can achieve essentially the same performance as the PairFormer.

Initial features.

Initial atom features for the trunk encode the charge, element, name and conformer reference position (giving a canonical geometry of individual residues, nucleotides and small molecules in isolation). These features are then processed and pooled to the token level. Additional initial token features are added to represent residue or nucleotide identity (for protein and nucleic acid chains), as well as coarse summaries of the MSA features (for protein chains). The token input feature width of 455 is the concatenation of a 384-dimensional aggregated atom encoding, a 33-dimensional residue-type encoding, a 34-dimensional coarse MSA feature vector, and four un-used channels.

Given this feature vector fif_{i}, the single and pair representations are initialized as

si(0)\displaystyle s_{i}^{(0)} =Ws​fi,\displaystyle=W_{s}f_{i}, (4.5)
zi​j(0)\displaystyle z_{ij}^{(0)} =Wa​fi+Wb​fj+ri​j+bi​jbond,\displaystyle=W_{a}f_{i}+W_{b}f_{j}+r_{ij}+b_{ij}^{\mathrm{bond}},

where ri​jr_{ij} encodes information about the relative positions of i,ji,j such as whether they belong to the same chain or entity and their sequence separation and bi​jbondb^{\text{bond}}_{ij} carries covalent bond information.

Mode conditioning.

The sampling mode mm distinguishes MD-conditioned equilibrium emulation from non-MD structure prediction. We implement this as a learned bias vector that is added to each token’s initial single representation and a second bias that is added to the initial pair representation.

Contact conditioning.

Following Boltz2 [39], the contact input is a list of token pairs and distance thresholds,

ℋ={(i,j,di​jmax)}.\mathcal{H}=\{(i,j,d_{ij}^{\max})\}. (4.6)

Each supplied pair is expected to lie within its threshold. The list is converted into pairwise features: a category distinguishes selected contacts, unselected pairs, and absence of contact conditioning. The learned contact bias added to the pair representation is denoted bi​jcontactb_{ij}^{\mathrm{contact}}. For a selected pair,

bi​jcontact=Embedcontact⁡(categoryi​j,di​jmax),b_{ij}^{\mathrm{contact}}=\operatorname{Embed}_{\mathrm{contact}}(\text{category}_{ij},d_{ij}^{\max}), (4.7)

the pair (j,i)(j,i) is updated symmetrically. Contact conditioning in the trunk is distinct from steering, the latter being an inference-time means of influencing the sampling process.

MSA input.

Initial MSA features for row rr at token ii contain a one-hot encoding of the residue (or gap), and flags for insertion, deletion and pairing. Given these MSA features ur​iu_{ri}, we combine them with initial token features fif_{i} via

Mr​i(0)=WM​ur​i+Wf​fi.M_{ri}^{(0)}=W_{M}u_{ri}+W_{f}f_{i}. (4.8)

Trunk layers.

The trunk uses an MSA module followed by a PairMixer stack [62]. The MSA module couples sequence rows through pair-conditioned averaging and transfers alignment information to pairs through outer-product aggregation. After 4 MSA layers, the subsequent 48 PairMixer layers operate only on the pair representation.

Both the MSA module and PairMixer use triangle multiplication, combining information about pairs that share an intermediate token. Suppressing learned projections, gates, and normalization, the two triangle operations have the form

Δ​zi​jout∼∑kA⁡(zi​k)⊙B⁡(zj​k),Δ​zi​jin∼∑kA′​(zk​i)⊙B′​(zk​j),\Delta z_{ij}^{\mathrm{out}}\sim\sum_{k}A(z_{ik})\odot B(z_{jk}),\qquad\Delta z_{ij}^{\mathrm{in}}\sim\sum_{k}A^{\prime}(z_{ki})\odot B^{\prime}(z_{kj}), (4.9)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. These operations communicate through triplets of tokens, allowing local chemical and evolutionary evidence to inform relationships across the system. PairMixer combines outgoing and incoming triangle updates with pair-wise transition networks, without triangle-attention layers [62]. The main stack refines pair features; single-token features retain their input- and mode-dependent information.

Recycling.

We repeat the MSA and pair-processing stages while feeding normalized, projected single and pair representations back into their initial states. We use 3 recycling steps by default at inference time. At training time, we use a deterministic schedule over recycling steps that keeps all ranks in sync.

4.4 Structure Module and Sampling

Dual-stream structure architecture.

Our structure module is closely inspired by the Flow Blocks introduced by NeuralPLexer3 [64]. Each of its 16 blocks interleaves atom-level and token-level updates, rather than separating atom encoding, a token transformer, and atom decoding as in AlphaFold 3 [5].

The atom stream uses windowed attention and transition MLPs; the token stream uses full token attention and transition MLPs. Cross-stream updates gather features at designated token-center atoms and broadcast token features to their associated atoms. Both streams are conditioned on the trunk representations and diffusion noise level. For time propagation, lag-time features and the supplied starting coordinates provide additional conditioning. A coordinate readout follows the stack, and EDM preconditioning combines this update with the noisy input to obtain a denoised coordinate estimate.

Conditional denoising.

After the biomolecular system has been embedded by the sequence trunk, BioEmu2’s structure model generates structures using a conditional diffusion model. The conditions are defined as follows:

𝒞=(𝒮,Esingle,Epair,[xt,τ]),\mathcal{C}=\left(\mathcal{S},E_{\mathrm{single}},E_{\mathrm{pair}};[x_{t},\tau]\right), (4.10)
  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S}: the static system features described under system embedding.

  • •

    EsingleE_{\mathrm{single}} and EpairE_{\mathrm{pair}}: the single-token and token-pair embeddings produced by the sequence trunk.

  • •

    [xt,τ][x_{t},\tau]: the optional configuration at an initial physical time and the positive lag τ\tau for time propagation. When supplied with equilibrium-mode conditioning, these specify sampling of a future endpoint xt+τx_{t+\tau} conditional on xtx_{t}.

The diffusion model is a conditional score model over all-atom Cartesian coordinates. At each denoising step, it receives the current noisy coordinates xnoisyx_{\text{noisy}} and their noise level σ\sigma, in addition to 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The static system features and embeddings are cached across steps. The score estimates the gradient of the logarithm of the noise-perturbed conditional density,

sθ​(xnoisy,σ∣𝒞)≈∇xnoisy​log​pσ​(xnoisy∣𝒞),s_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy}},\sigma\mid\mathcal{C})\approx\nabla_{x_{\text{noisy}}}\log p_{\sigma}(x_{\text{noisy}}\mid\mathcal{C}), (4.11)

where pσp_{\sigma} is the target structural distribution convolved with Gaussian noise of covariance σ2​I\sigma^{2}I. BioEmu2 uses a denoiser parameterization [65]: the network reconstructs clean coordinates Dθ​(xnoisy,σ∣𝒞)D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy}},\sigma\mid\mathcal{C}), which define the score through

sθ​(xnoisy,σ∣𝒞)=Dθ​(xnoisy,σ∣𝒞)−xnoisyσ2.s_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy}},\sigma\mid\mathcal{C})=\frac{D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy}},\sigma\mid\mathcal{C})-x_{\text{noisy}}}{\sigma^{2}}. (4.12)

Sampling from the model means progressively denoising the structure. It starts from Gaussian coordinates xnoisy,σmax∼𝒩⁡(0,σmax2​I)x_{\text{noisy},\sigma_{\max}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\max}^{2}I) and progressively denoises them along a decreasing noise schedule [65]. Without ITO conditioning, the result is a sample from the selected structural distribution. With xtx_{t} and τ\tau, the result is a future configuration xt+τx_{t+\tau}. (The noise level σ\sigma and the sampler’s denoising steps are distinct from the physical lag τ\tau.)

Treatment of the ITO inputs.

The time-conditioning inputs, [xt,τ][x_{t},\tau], enter only via the structure module. At training time, we apply noise N⁡(0,ς2)N(0,\varsigma^{2}) to the structure xtx_{t} to improve the model’s robustness to errors in the original structure (ς=0.1\varsigma=0.1Å). We featurize τ\tau via ek(τ)=e−τ/sk{1,sin(2πqτ/sk),cos(2πqτ/sk)}e_{k}(\tau)=e^{-\tau/s_{k}}\{1,\sin(2\pi q\tau/s_{k}),\cos(2\pi q\tau/s_{k})\} concatenated over various decay rates sks_{k} and various qq. These features enter the single conditioning stream alongside the diffusion noise scale embedding. The time-conditioning coordinates xtx_{t} enter alongside the noisy coordinates xnoisyx_{\text{noisy}}, and are multiplied by a gate g⁡(τ)g(\tau) which is constructed so that g→0g\to 0 as τ→∞\tau\to\infty.

EDM preconditioning and inference updates.

We follow the EDM diffusion model set-up [65]. Writing Δ​xθ\Delta x_{\theta} for the network’s coordinate-update readout, the EDM denoiser [65] is

Dθ​(xnoisy,σ∣𝒞)=cskip​(σ)​xnoisy+cout​(σ)​Δ​xθ​(cin​(σ)​xnoisy,cnoise​(σ)∣𝒞),D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy}},\sigma\mid\mathcal{C})=c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\sigma)x_{\text{noisy}}+c_{\mathrm{out}}(\sigma)\Delta x_{\theta}(c_{\mathrm{in}}(\sigma)x_{\text{noisy}},c_{\mathrm{noise}}(\sigma)\mid\mathcal{C}), (4.13)

with

cskip​(σ)\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\sigma) =σdata2σ2+σdata2,\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}+\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^{2}}, cout​(σ)\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{out}}(\sigma) =σ​σdataσ2+σdata2,\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^{2}}}, (4.14)
cin​(σ)\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{in}}(\sigma) =1σ2+σdata2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^{2}}}, cnoise​(σ)\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{noise}}(\sigma) =14​log⁡σσdata.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}}.

Here, σdata\sigma_{\mathrm{data}} sets the coordinate scale used for preconditioning, 16Å in our case.

Let σ0>⋯>σK=0\sigma_{0}>\cdots>\sigma_{K}=0 be the inference noise schedule, and let x(0)∼𝒩⁡(0,σ02​I)x^{(0)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}I). At step kk, noise injection (“churn”) temporarily increases the noise level,

σ^k=(1+γk)​σk,xnoisy,k=x(k)+Snoise​σ^k2−σk2​ϵk,ϵk∼𝒩⁡(0,I).\widehat{\sigma}_{k}=(1+\gamma_{k})\sigma_{k},\qquad x_{\text{noisy},k}=x^{(k)}+S_{\mathrm{noise}}\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{2}-\sigma_{k}^{2}}\,\epsilon_{k},\qquad\epsilon_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (4.15)

We switch off churn below a certain noise level, simply setting xnoisy,k=x(k)x_{\text{noisy},k}=x^{(k)} and σ^k=σk\widehat{\sigma}_{k}=\sigma_{k}. Given the structure xnoisy,kx_{\text{noisy},k}, one denoiser evaluation gives x^k=Dθ​(xnoisy,k,σ^k∣𝒞)\widehat{x}_{k}=D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy},k},\widehat{\sigma}_{k}\mid\mathcal{C}), followed by

xupdate,k=xnoisy,k−x^kσ^k,x(k+1)=xnoisy,k+Sstep​(σk+1−σ^k)​xupdate,k.x_{\text{update},k}=\frac{x_{\text{noisy},k}-\widehat{x}_{k}}{\widehat{\sigma}_{k}},\qquad x^{(k+1)}=x_{\text{noisy},k}+S_{\text{step}}(\sigma_{k+1}-\widehat{\sigma}_{k})x_{\text{update},k}. (4.16)

Global rigid augmentations are applied at each step. If an ITO conditioning structure xtx_{t} is used, the same rigid augmentations are applied to it. At inference, as in AF3, the noisy coordinates at each reverse step are rigidly aligned to the denoised prediction before the update in (4.16).

With direct steering, x^k\widehat{x}_{k} is replaced by a guided denoised estimate before computing xupdate,kx_{\text{update},k}. The corresponding equations and particle-correction variants are given in Sec. 4.7.

Structure-prediction sharpening.

For structure prediction, we apply empirical sharpening in the EDM sampling framework [65] by amplifying the denoising updates relative to the injected noise. In the update above, this corresponds to setting Sstep=1.5,Snoise=1.003S_{\text{step}}=1.5,S_{\text{noise}}=1.003 in equation (4.16), compared with Sstep=Snoise=1S_{\text{step}}=S_{\text{noise}}=1 for equilibrium sampling. The structure prediction modification is also used in AlphaFold 3 [5] and Boltz [28, 39].

4.5 Sampling the Equilibrium Distribution

Our MD simulations use the isothermal-isobaric, or N​p​TNpT, ensemble: particle number NN, external pressure pp, and temperature TT are fixed, while the simulation volume VV fluctuates. BioEmu2 targets equilibrium sampling at ambient conditions: the N​p​TNpT training simulations used room temperature TT and a pressure of p=1p=1 atm. Let xx denote the biomolecular coordinates generated by BioEmu2, and let zz collect the remaining configurational degrees of freedom, including explicit solvent. After integrating out momenta, the dimensionless reduced energy of the full configuration is

u⁡(x,z,V)=β⁡[U⁡(x,z,V)+p​V],β=1kB​T,u(x,z,V)=\beta\left[U(x,z;V)+pV\right],\qquad\beta=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}, (4.17)

where UU is the potential energy and kBk_{\mathrm{B}} is Boltzmann’s constant. The joint equilibrium density is

ρ⁡(x,z,V)=Z−1​exp⁡[−u⁡(x,z,V)],\rho(x,z,V)=Z^{-1}\exp[-u(x,z,V)], (4.18)

with normalization constant ZZ and the volume-dependent Cartesian configuration domain understood. The equilibrium distribution relevant to the model is the marginal over solvent and volume,

pe​q​(x)=∫0∞d​V​∫d​z​ρ​(x,z,V).p_{eq}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}V\int\mathrm{d}z\,\rho(x,z,V). (4.19)

BioEmu2 therefore includes solvent effects implicitly: it generates biomolecular coordinates without explicit solvent coordinates, while learning a distribution in which solvent and volume degrees of freedom have been marginalized out. Thus, the structural distribution is not simply the Boltzmann factor of an isolated protein.

BioEmu2 is a Boltzmann emulator which approximates this equilibrium distribution by

x∼pθ,pθ​(x)≈pe​q​(x),x\sim p_{\theta},\qquad p_{\theta}(x)\approx p_{eq}(x), (4.20)

where θ\theta denotes shared learned parameters and the dependence on the system’s sequence embeddings is suppressed for readability. Equilibrium sampling is an approximation objective, not a guarantee of calibrated populations or quantitative free energies for every system.

4.6 Time Propagation

Markov state models (MSMs) describe molecular kinetics as transitions between discrete conformational states at a chosen lag time τ\tau [66, 67, 68]. When many short trajectories collectively sample the relevant states and transitions, MSMs can recover long-time relaxation and equilibrium populations without requiring each trajectory to equilibrate [67, 68]. Conventional MSMs, however, are system-specific analysis models and do not transfer across molecular systems.

More recent work has turned to generative neural networks, which can generalize across molecular systems. Examples include deep generative MSMs [69], Timewarp [25], MDGen [26], and transferable extensions of the implicit transfer operator (ITO) framework [48, 70]. BioEmu2 follows the original ITO formulation [27], in which a diffusion model conditioned on starting coordinates xtx_{t} and a physical lag τ\tau samples

xt+τ∼pθ,τ(⋅∣xt),x_{t+\tau}\sim p_{\theta,\tau}(\,\cdot\mid x_{t}), (4.21)

approximating the physical transition density pτ​(xt+τ∣xt)p_{\tau}(x_{t+\tau}\mid x_{t}). This formulation allows BioEmu2 to generate the endpoint xt+τx_{t+\tau} directly, without resolving the intervening MD trajectory. Long-running, time-ordered trajectories can be sampled by repeated conditional sampling. Because only biomolecular coordinates are retained, other dynamical degrees of freedom, such as momenta and solvent, are generally not carried from one step to the next.

Equilibrium limit.

For ergodic systems, dynamics relax to a unique equilibrium distribution and the physical transition density loses memory of its initial configuration. For the model, the corresponding consistency condition is

limτ→∞pθ,τ​(xt+τ∣xt)=pθ​(xt+τ),\lim_{\tau\to\infty}p_{\theta,\tau}(x_{t+\tau}\mid x_{t})=p_{\theta}(x_{t+\tau}), (4.22)

where pθp_{\theta} is the equilibrium model as noted in Eq. (4.20). We impose consistency with the empirical equilibrium defined by the molecular dynamics training data, rather than infer equilibrium from transitions as in MSMs.

To achieve this, we follow ideas from BoPITO [71] and separate the transition density into a stationary part, given by the equilibrium model, and a time-dependent part that decays with the lag. In practice, the network does not add separate equilibrium and dynamic scores. Instead, it removes the time-dependent part by fading out its dynamics conditioning as the lag grows. The lag-time features carry exponential envelopes ek​(τ)e_{k}(\tau) and conditioning on the initial configuration is gated by a learned positive combination of these envelopes:

ek(τ)=exp(−τ/sk),g(τ)=∑kwkek(τ),wk>0,0<sk≤smax.e_{k}(\tau)=\exp(-\tau/s_{k}),\qquad g(\tau)=\sum_{k}w_{k}e_{k}(\tau),\qquad w_{k}>0,\quad 0<s_{k}\leq s_{\max}. (4.23)

The lag-time embedding added to the single representation takes the form of a damped harmonic oscillator and decays on the same timescales. With smax=1s_{\max}=1 ms, both the gate and the lag-time embedding vanish for τ≫smax\tau\gg s_{\max}, so only the stationary part remains and the network recovers the equilibrium denoiser exactly. The form of this crossover is an architectural choice, but the weights wkw_{k} and timescales sks_{k} are learned from data. The crossover should therefore not be read as an estimate of a physical relaxation time: It guarantees consistency with the learned equilibrium distribution, which need not coincide with exact thermodynamic equilibrium.

Training.

For a fraction of the training samples, we draw pairs of frames (xt,xt+τ)(x_{t},x_{t+\tau}) from the same MD trajectory. We rigidly align the target frame to the starting frame, then apply the same random rotation and translation to both, which preserves the motion relative to the starting configuration. The remaining MD frames serve as independent equilibrium examples, with dynamics conditioning masked out and the lag set to τ=∞\tau=\infty. Both tasks share the same network and EDM denoising loss (Sec. 4.4).

Nearly all of BioEmu2’s dynamics training data comes from MD simulations of up to 1​μ​s1\,\mu\mathrm{s}. Rates and pathways predicted for slower processes, such as binding, dissociation, folding, unfolding and other slow rearrangements, therefore require independent validation. Until the model is trained and validated on experimental data at these timescales, such predictions should be treated as qualitative hypotheses rather than quantitative kinetics.

Rollouts.

Each ITO step runs the full diffusion sampler, with every denoiser evaluation conditioned on the preceding configuration xtx_{t} and the chosen lag τ\tau, while the trunk embeddings are computed once per system and reused across steps. With fixed sampler settings, the cost per step is independent of τ\tau, and the required compute grows linearly with the simulation time. The lag can vary between steps, and starting configurations can be experimental or predicted structures, equilibrium samples, or manually modified structures, such as an apo protein with ligands placed next to it.

4.7 Steering and Enhanced Sampling

Steering changes the structural distribution sampled at inference time without retraining the model. Unlike mode or contact conditioning, which changes the trunk embeddings, it acts on coordinate generation. It can favour physical geometry, particular conformations, or regions that are rare under the unsteered model. BioEmu2 implements potential-gradient guidance and particle-based Feynman-Kac methods [53, 57, 54], which can also support enhanced-sampling workflows [52].

Potentials and the tilted distribution.

Let pbase​(x)p_{\mathrm{base}}(x) denote the unsteered distribution for fixed system and conditioning. A dimensionless potential v⁡(x)v(x) specifies the desired tilt,

pv​(x)=Zv−1​pbase​(x)​exp​[−v⁡(x)],Zv=∫pbase​(x)​exp​[−v⁡(x)]​𝑑x.p_{v}(x)=Z_{v}^{-1}p_{\mathrm{base}}(x)\exp[-v(x)],\qquad Z_{v}=\int p_{\mathrm{base}}(x)\exp[-v(x)]\,\mathrm{d}x. (4.24)

Lower potential values are favored. For a physical bias energy B⁡(x)B(x), the corresponding dimensionless potential is v⁡(x)=β​B​(x)v(x)=\beta B(x); geometric penalties can instead be defined directly in dimensionless form. Multiple objectives can be combined by summing their potentials. The tilt defines a target distribution, not a guarantee that every guidance procedure samples it exactly.

Coordinate notation.

Following the notation of Section 4.4, ii indexes denoising steps rather than physical time. The coordinates x(i)x^{(i)} are the current noisy state at scheduled noise level σi\sigma_{i}; xnoisy,ix_{\text{noisy},i} denotes the coordinates after augmentation and noise injection, at reheated noise level σ^i\hat{\sigma}_{i}; and x^i=Dθ​(xnoisy,i,σ^i∣C)\hat{x}_{i}=D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy},i},\hat{\sigma}_{i}\mid C) is the corresponding prediction of clean coordinates with conditioning CC. We omit the particle index. The two procedures use these same coordinates but differ in their reheating schedules and in where the gradient is taken.

Physicality steering: geometry penalties.

Physicality potentials discourage local geometric defects during coordinate generation. We adapt the Boltz-steering potentials [28] for ligand distance geometry, chirality, bond stereochemistry, planarity, and chain overlap, and extend them with explicit bond-length and bond-angle restraints and polymer clash penalties. The polymer clash penalties discourage atomic clashes within and between chains. The general intra-chain and inter-chain clash penalties exclude atom pairs connected within three covalent bonds. A separate local penalty prevents excessively close contacts between eligible protein or nucleic-acid atoms in different residues that are connected by two or three bonds. The geometry restraints use tabulated reference values, including peptide and nucleotide linkages and declared disulfide bonds, with broad bounds where a matching reference is unavailable.

Following Boltz-steering, admissible intervals can be enforced with a flat-bottom penalty. A one-sided constraint omits the corresponding bound term. The violation vanishes within the allowed interval and grows linearly outside it; potential-specific scaling and sampler coefficients determine its influence. For a scalar geometric quantity qq with lower and upper bounds qminq_{\min} and qmaxq_{\max}, the unweighted violation is

h⁡(q,qmin,qmax)=max⁡(qmin−q,0)+max⁡(q−qmax,0).h(q;q_{\min},q_{\max})=\max(q_{\min}-q,0)+\max(q-q_{\max},0). (4.25)

Other potentials can favour a specified contact, reference conformation, or collective-variable range.

Physicality steering: detached-coordinate guidance.

We use the churn schedule of Section 4.4 and evaluate x^i\hat{x}_{i} without differentiating through the denoiser. At each guided diffusion step, we initialize a separate optimization variable yi(0)=x^iy_{i}^{(0)}=\hat{x}_{i}. Here ℓ\ell counts inner potential-gradient steps, not diffusion steps, and jj indexes the potentials:

yi(ℓ+1)=yi(ℓ)−∑jηj,i,ℓ​∇yUj​(yi(ℓ)),x^ig=yi(Li).y_{i}^{(\ell+1)}=y_{i}^{(\ell)}-\sum_{j}\eta_{j,i,\ell}\nabla_{y}U_{j}(y_{i}^{(\ell)}),\qquad\hat{x}_{i}^{\,g}=y_{i}^{(L_{i})}. (4.26)

After LiL_{i} inner steps, x^ig=yi(Li)\hat{x}_{i}^{\,g}=y_{i}^{(L_{i})} is the guided clean-coordinate prediction; the superscript gg denotes guidance. The coefficients ηj,i,ℓ\eta_{j,i,\ell} include each potential’s guidance strength and activation schedule, and guidance is applied on nonterminal transitions. We then apply the EDM update in Eq. 4.16, substituting the guided clean prediction x^ig\hat{x}_{i}^{g} for x^i\hat{x}_{i}. If resampling is enabled, each selected particle carries forward both its noisy coordinates and its guided prediction. If rigid alignment is enabled, we first align those noisy coordinates to that prediction.

Thus, the potential modifies the denoised prediction used for transport rather than backpropagating through the denoiser to its noisy input. Optional FK resampling uses differences of weighted potential energies evaluated before guidance, multiplied by a global weighting strength, together with a correction based on the carried guidance displacement and the current Gaussian noise.

For the physicality comparison in Fig. 6b, we used detached-coordinate gradient guidance without particle resampling, active during approximately the final 20% of 200 denoising transitions. The sampling cohort and evaluation procedures are described in Section 4.8. Better local geometry does not guarantee better equilibrium populations, but helps to preserve and improve structure prediction metrics while significantly reduces unphysicalities.

Enhanced sampling: through-denoiser guidance and TDS weights.

For the PGK example, we instead use Twisted Diffusion Sampler (TDS) [54]. Let vi​(x)v_{i}(x) be the bias on clean coordinates at step ii, including any step-dependent scaling or changes to its parameters. The corresponding bias on noisy coordinates is Vi​(xnoisy)=vi​(Dθ​(xnoisy,σ^i∣C))V_{i}(x_{\text{noisy}})=v_{i}(D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy}},\hat{\sigma}_{i}\mid C)). Here ViV_{i} is a function of noisy input coordinates through the denoiser, unlike the physicality optimization over detached yy. We use sigma reheating rather than the physicality churn schedule: σ^0=σ0\hat{\sigma}_{0}=\sigma_{0} and σ^i=σi−1\hat{\sigma}_{i}=\sigma_{i-1} for i>0i>0, with injected-noise variance νi=σ^i2−σi2\nu_{i}=\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{2}-\sigma_{i}^{2}. With Sstep=1S_{\text{step}}=1, the nonterminal proposal is

x(i+1)=xnoisy,i+σ^i−σi+1σ^i​[Dθ​(xnoisy,i,σ^i∣C)−xnoisy,i]−νi2​∇xnoisy,iVi​(xnoisy,i),x^{(i+1)}=x_{\text{noisy},i}+\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{i}-\sigma_{i+1}}{\hat{\sigma}_{i}}\left[D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy},i},\hat{\sigma}_{i}\mid C)-x_{\text{noisy},i}\right]-\frac{\nu_{i}}{2}\nabla_{x_{\text{noisy},i}}V_{i}(x_{\text{noisy},i}), (4.27)

The gradient acts on the noisy coordinates xnoisy,ix_{\text{noisy},i} through the denoiser. Let wiw_{i} denote an unnormalized particle weight at reheated state xnoisy,ix_{\text{noisy},i}. The log weights accumulate between resampling events according to

log⁡wi=log⁡wi−1−Vi​(xnoisy,i)+Vi−1​(xnoisy,i−1)+log⁡KiQi,i≥1.\log w_{i}=\log w_{i-1}-V_{i}(x_{\text{noisy},i})+V_{i-1}(x_{\text{noisy},{i-1}})+\log\frac{K_{i}}{Q_{i}},\qquad i\geq 1. (4.28)

Here KiK_{i} and QiQ_{i} are the reference and guided-proposal transition densities evaluated at xnoisy,ix_{\text{noisy},i}. They combine the preceding unguided or guided transport, respectively, with the current Gaussian refresh, conditional on the same sampled rigid augmentation. If their means differ by δi=mQ,i−mK,i\delta_{i}=m_{Q,i}-m_{K,i} and ri=xnoisy,i−mQ,ir_{i}=x_{\text{noisy},i}-m_{Q,i} is the sampled Gaussian residual, then log(Ki/Qi)=−ri𝖳δi/νi−∥δi∥2/(2νi)\log(K_{i}/Q_{i})=-r_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\delta_{i}/\nu_{i}-\|\delta_{i}\|^{2}/(2\nu_{i}). The means are centered separately before applying the shared rotation and translation.

The initial log weight is −V0​(xnoisy,0)-V_{0}(x_{\text{noisy},0}), which need not vanish for constant-strength steering. On the last transition mm, σm+1=0\sigma_{m+1}=0 and guidance is disabled. Setting the guidance term to zero in Eq. 4.27, with a=1a=1, gives the completed sample X=x(m+1)=Dθ​(xnoisy,m,σ^m∣C)X=x^{(m+1)}=D_{\theta}(x_{\text{noisy},m},\hat{\sigma}_{m}\mid C); the final log-weight increment is −v⁡(X)+Vm​(xnoisy,m)-v(X)+V_{m}(x_{\text{noisy},m}). The resulting target is pv​(X)∝pθ​(X)​e−v⁡(X)p_{v}(X)\propto p_{\theta}(X)e^{-v(X)}, where pθp_{\theta} is the endpoint distribution of the finite-step unguided reference sampler. Finite particle populations and weight degeneracy limit estimation of this target. Our PGK example used the discrete TDS kernel ratio in Eq. 4.28 [54], not the Feynman–Kac Corrector (FKC) weight rule [57] as in the previous work [52]. Unlike FKC, the TDS rule does not require ∂σU\partial_{\sigma}U, a noise-level derivative of the potential through the denoiser.

Enhanced sampling: particle resampling.

We normalize weights within each particle group and compute Neff=1/∑n=1Npw¯n2N_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\sum_{n=1}^{N_{p}}\bar{w}_{n}^{2}. The TDS implementation supports resampling at a configured interval or when any group’s fraction Neff/NpN_{\mathrm{eff}}/N_{p} falls below a threshold. Systematic resampling copies all ancestry-dependent state and resets the accumulated log weights; a final resampling is performed when potentials are supplied. The returned particles have equal weights but can share ancestors and should not be counted as independent observations.

Enhanced sampling: recovering unbiased model statistics.

A bias potential can favor conformations that the unsteered model samples only rarely [52]. In the tilted ensemble, the probability of a structure xx is proportional to its unsteered probability pbase​(x)p_{\mathrm{base}}(x) multiplied by exp⁡[−v⁡(x)]\exp[-v(x)]. With sufficient overlap between the biased and unsteered ensembles, we can therefore estimate the unsteered mean of an observable AA by weighting each structure by the inverse factor:

⟨A⟩base=⟨A⁡(x)​exp⁡[v⁡(x)]⟩v⟨exp⁡[v⁡(x)]⟩v.\langle A\rangle_{\mathrm{base}}=\frac{\langle A(x)\exp[v(x)]\rangle_{v}}{\langle\exp[v(x)]\rangle_{v}}. (4.29)

When multiple windows are used to apply different biases, their relative normalizations can be estimated with multistate reweighting using MBAR [60]. We remark that the steering and reweighting method can address rare-event sampling to recover statistics of the base model; they do not remove errors in the base model itself.

Example: PGK domain-pose enhanced sampling.

To illustrate how a known alternative conformation can guide exploration without prescribing its population, we sampled apo PGK with equilibrium-mode conditioning and biased the relative translation and rotation of its N- and C-domain cores toward the closed reference 2X13. The results are shown in Fig. 6c. We fitted the centered closed-reference cores to the corresponding sampled C-alpha coordinates, using 164 N-core and 186 C-core atoms. Let RN,RCR_{N},R_{C} be the proper fitted rotations in row-vector convention, cN,cCc_{N},c_{C} the sampled core centroids, and cN⋆,cC⋆c_{N}^{\star},c_{C}^{\star} their closed-reference centroids. The bias collective variables are the translation error in the N-core frame and the relative-rotation chord error:

d⁡(X)=‖(cC−cN)​RN𝖳−(cC⋆−cN⋆)‖,c⁡(X)=‖RC​RN𝖳−I‖F2.d(X)=\left\|(c_{C}-c_{N})R_{N}^{\mathsf{T}}-(c_{C}^{\star}-c_{N}^{\star})\right\|,\qquad c(X)=\frac{\left\|R_{C}R_{N}^{\mathsf{T}}-I\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}}{\sqrt{2}}. (4.30)

For a window with strength kk, the bias v⁡(X,k)v(X;k) is quadratic outside the flat-bottom tolerances:

v⁡(X,k)=k2​[([d⁡(X)−d0]+wd)2+([c⁡(X)−c0]+wc)2],[u]+=max⁡(u,0).v(X;k)=\frac{k}{2}\left[\left(\frac{[d(X)-d_{0}]_{+}}{w_{d}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{[c(X)-c_{0}]_{+}}{w_{c}}\right)^{2}\right],\qquad[u]_{+}=\max(u,0). (4.31)

We used d0=1​Åd_{0}=1\,\mathrm{\AA}, wd=2​Åw_{d}=2\,\mathrm{\AA}, c0=2​sin⁡(5∘/2)c_{0}=2\sin(5^{\circ}/2), and wc=2​sin⁡(15∘/2)w_{c}=2\sin(15^{\circ}/2). This restrains the fitted interdomain pose rather than directly penalizing internal core RMSDs. We used two biased windows, k=0.5k=0.5 and k=1k=1, with TDS weights and 200 diffusion transitions per 14-particle population. Systematic resampling was triggered when Neff/14<0.5N_{\mathrm{eff}}/14<0.5 and was also performed at the final endpoint. All 1,008 returned structures at each nonzero strength were retained without RMSD-based population screening.

For visualization, we computed independently rigid-aligned C-alpha RMSDs to open 2XE7 and closed 2X13 over a common 406-atom selection. The baseline panel (Fig. 6c left) contains 4,032 unsteered structures. The enhanced panel (Fig. 6c right) estimates the unbiased (i.e. k=0k=0) distribution by ordinary MBAR [60], pooling 2,016 baseline structures with the 1,008 structures from each steered ensemble with k=0.5k=0.5 and k=1k=1. We evaluated each saved structure under all three bias conditions, k=0,0.5,1k=0,0.5,1, and supplied these bias energies and the sample counts to MBAR, which computes separate weights for estimating unbiased baseline statistics. The free energy landscapes are rendered as contours of Δ​F=−R​T​log⁡(p/pmax)\Delta F=-RT\log(p/p_{\max}), with T=300​KT=300\,\mathrm{K}.

The representative structures A-C were selected from saved source-pool frames in designated regions of this projection, subject to the protein geometry quality checks. These selections did not filter the landscapes. The structural illustrations use an N-core alignment and a common camera and scale, whereas the plotted RMSDs use independent whole-protein alignments to each reference.

4.8 Benchmark Details

Structure prediction benchmarks.

We evaluated structure prediction using variations of FoldBench and Runs N’ Poses. FoldBench covers protein and nucleic-acid monomers and six molecular-interface categories [32]; Runs N’ Poses evaluates protein–ligand co-folding across ligand–pocket similarity strata [33].

To ensure complete uniformity between competing methods, we decided to resample locally over the same task definition and MSAs, and then feed the samples to a common OpenStructure (OST) v2.11.1 pipeline [72]. For every included model, we generated new predictions from the adapted tasks with the default prediction setup in publicly available code. AlphaFold3 [5] was omitted for licensing reasons, and Boltz-2 [39] because of its later training cut-off date. ColabFold-based MSA variants were used where available [35]; ESMFold2-Fast was evaluated without MSAs [31].

FoldBench sampling tasks were converted via the AlphaFold3 pipeline following the authors’ descriptions [32]. Runs N’ Poses system definitions retained the upstream protein and ligand entities, using CCD definitions where possible and SMILES otherwise (e.g. for glycan chains or peptides). 32 FoldBench systems are excluded due to common OST errors (14), common ligand modelling issues (8), problematic raw PDB deposition info (5), and DNA/RNA hybrids (5). 39 Runs N’ Poses systems were excluded owing to upstream fixes in PLINDER (21), token count exceeding 2,560 causing issues to multiple baselines (10), common OST errors (6), and common ligand modelling issues (2). To avoid train–test pollution, we further removed 6 FoldBench and 584 Runs N’ Poses systems whose source PDB entries were deposited on or before 2021-09-30 but released afterward. The final set after all exclusions mentioned above serves as the shared denominator for success rate. Thus, unlike some other implementations of these benchmarks, we ensured that all models were compared on an identical set of test systems.

Comparisons used five generated structures per system. We start with sampling five structures in the same batch on NVIDIA A100-80GB GPUs, and out-of-memory cases were retried with lower batch-size and/or rerun on B200 GPUs.

For a fair comparison without a confidence ranker, all models were assessed using best-of-five (oracle) selection. Monomer performance was summarized by mean best-of-five lDDT. Non-ligand interface success required DockQ ≥0.23\geq 0.23; ligand success required RMSD <2<2 Å and lDDT-PLI >0.8>0.8 within a prediction. Runs N’ Poses scored annotated proper ligands separately according to source assignments. The upstream SuCOS-pocket similarity bins are used for binning and visualization, omitting ligands without pre-assigned numeric similarity. Uncertainty was estimated using 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals from 1,000 target-level resamples.

Polymer geometry evaluation.

For Fig. 6b, we compared five structures per sampling condition for each of 1,490 eligible systems. Accuracy uses the best-of-five criteria above; geometry includes all five structures, including those rejected by the saved filtering procedure. Both conditions were evaluated with identical OpenStructure 2.11.1 Scorer/Molck preparation and StereoCheck. A structure is counted as affected if at least one polymer clash, bond-length outlier, or bond-angle outlier is reported. Checks cover whole-system polymers and exclude ligand internal geometry and polymer-ligand clashes.

Geometry incidence is the affected fraction of the five structures from each unique system in a category, averaged across those systems. Categories may overlap. For this comparison, accuracy uses eligible interface or monomer target instances, with missing or unscorable targets counted as zero; these instances are the resampling units in the 1,000-replicate accuracy bootstrap. Geometry uses 5,000 paired system-bootstrap resamples, retaining all five structures and matching system identities between conditions, to obtain 95% percentile intervals. The sampling campaigns differ in source revision, compilation, and numerical settings, so the comparison is descriptive rather than an isolated causal ablation of guidance.
